part_title: Q Business Controls and Q Apps in Context
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 5 through 6 individually in source order, verifying visible labels, workflows, examples, access-control boundaries, and service distinctions; rewritten as balanced-length teaching narration.

scenes.title: Q Business admin controls
scenes.narration: This slide shows that Amazon Q Business administrators can shape what the assistant is allowed to answer, in addition to controlling who can read source documents. Start at the left with an employee asking, 'What is our travel policy?' Q Business applies the configured controls. First, the global response scope restricts answers to connected internal company content. Next, topic-level rules can block configured subjects, as the yellow box indicates. The right-hand section shows two kinds of outcomes: an allowed question produces a grounded answer from the permitted internal sources, while configured blocked words or phrases can cause a refusal. Look at the examples below. A travel-policy question uses company documents and receives a policy-based reply. A question about company merger-and-acquisition strategy triggers an illustrative topic block and receives 'I can't answer that question.' On the right, global response scope, topic-level block rules and blocked-word policies are separated because they solve different problems. The bottom note also distinguishes these Q Business chat controls from Bedrock Guardrails. Neither of these settings replaces document ACLs. Test rules so legitimate employee questions are not accidentally blocked and confidential information remains protected.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Apps
scenes.narration: Here we move from asking individual questions to building a reusable workflow. The user asks where to find onboarding guidance, and Amazon Q Business retrieves approved company documents from S3 or SharePoint. In the third panel, a user builds an Amazon Q App by describing an onboarding FAQ application in natural language and optionally adding fields such as topic and audience. Instead of repeating the same question manually, teammates can use this shared internal app. The final panel shows a grounded answer with the onboarding guide cited. The worked example below follows the same path: a teammate asks a question, the app consults company knowledge, and the answer includes its source. Now compare the two tools in the lower-right exam distinction. Amazon Q Apps are for reusable organization workflows that rely on internal content, controlled access and sharing. PartyRock is a different no-code playground for quickly experimenting with generative AI ideas. The useful decision question is whether this app needs governed company data and repeatable team use. If so, use the supported internal Q Apps approach rather than an experimental public prototype.
